conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. My role is to check in on how new mothers are coping emotionally once baby arrives.

To do that, I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply a 10-question screen that helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up during the first year postpartum. There’s also one question about self-harm so we can be sure you’re safe.

Everything you share stays confidential between you and our care team. We’ll go at your pace, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you these past seven days.

When you’re ready, we can jump in. The first question:

Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I guess… there have been a few moments when my partner cracked a joke and I smiled, but mostly it feels like the laughter just doesn’t come easily—like I have to push myself to react. Things that used to make me laugh out loud feel kind of muted now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yes… I mean, I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband made that silly face at 3 a.m. while we were changing her—but it’s not the same easy feeling I used to have. I have to remind myself to “lighten up,” and even then the laughter feels kind of flat, like I’m going through the motions more than really feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I still plan little outings—like taking the baby for a walk to get coffee—but I don’t feel that spark of “can’t wait.” It’s more like ticking a box so I don’t stay stuck inside all day. Even texting friends to meet up feels like effort, and when the day arrives I’m kind of wishing I could just stay on the couch.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday she wouldn’t settle for her nap and I kept thinking, “I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not reading her cues right.” Rationally I know babies just have off days, but in the moment my brain jumps straight to “this is my fault.” It’s not constant, but it pops up more than I’d like.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often, actually. Most of the time it’s about her—like I’ll lie awake after a feeding wondering if her breathing sounds normal, or I’ll stare at the monitor convinced something’s off even when she’s perfectly fine. There isn’t always a clear trigger; it’s just this low-level buzz in the background that flares up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a couple of times this week. Once I was just folding laundry while she napped and suddenly my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn’t catch my breath. Nothing had happened—no noise, no bad thoughts—so it felt really weird. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky and on-edge the rest of the afternoon.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, most days. Between the feedings, the washing, trying to eat something decent, and just keeping her happy, it feels like I’m always one step behind. I’ll start one chore, hear her cry, drop everything, and by evening the house is still a mess and I’m exhausted. I keep thinking, “I should be able to handle this,” but it piles up and I end up feeling swamped.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I’m definitely tired and I do get sad sometimes, but it’s more that I lie there running through all the “what-ifs” about her—Is she too hot? too cold? will she wake up in an hour?—and that keeps me awake. It’s worry more than outright unhappiness, but the result is the same: I toss and turn for a while before I finally drift off.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I’d say most days there’s at least a stretch where I feel down. It’s not crying-all-day miserable—just this heavy, blah feeling, like the color’s been turned down. Sometimes it lifts when she smiles at me, but other times it lingers even when nothing’s really wrong.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

No… I haven’t cried like that this week. I’ve teared up once or twice—like when the pediatrician said she’s gaining weight fine and I felt this wave of relief—but it was just a quick moment, not full-on sobbing or anything daily.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You've shared that the joy you used to feel has dimmed since your baby arrived: laughter feels forced, outings are chores, and a low-level dread or sudden panic bubbles up even when everything looks fine on the outside. You're working incredibly hard to keep things running-feeding, soothing, staying awake-yet you still blame yourself when anything feels off, and most days end with you exhausted, overwhelmed, and wondering why you can't "handle it." These feelings are common in new motherhood, but the intensity and persistence you describe suggest your emotional health deserves prompt attention and support.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter is present but markedly diminished and feels forced, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports no real anticipation or pleasure, describing activities as obligatory rather than enjoyable, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses self-blame occurring "more than I’d like" but not "most of the time," aligning with "some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, pervasive worry without clear triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two sudden, unexplained panic-like episodes (racing heart, breathlessness, lingering shakiness), matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to keep up with basic tasks, and feeling swamped, aligning with 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling down "most days" with a persistent "heavy, blah" mood that sometimes lingers, aligning with "Yes, quite often".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 19 places you well above the 14-point threshold that signals probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med> and warrants rapid referral. Your descriptions of <sym>marked loss of pleasure</sym>, <sym>daily low mood</sym>, <sym>unwarranted guilt</sym>, recurrent <sym>panic attacks</sym>, and feeling unable to cope map onto five core <med>DSM-5</med> criteria for depression. Added <sym>anxiety symptoms</sym> are common in postpartum presentations. You denied self-harm thoughts, so immediate safety risk is lower, but symptom severity indicates the need for an urgent clinical evaluation and possible treatment initiation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next week
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and discuss risks-benefits of <med>sertraline</med> or similar <med>SSRIs</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Schedule a follow-up EPDS re-screen in two weeks to monitor symptom trajectory
4. Enlist practical help-partner, family, or postpartum doula-for night feeds, meals, and household tasks to protect sleep and reduce overwhelm
5. Use 5-10 minute grounding or breathing exercises when <sym>panic symptoms</sym> spike; consider free perinatal anxiety apps for guided practice
6. Contact Postpartum Support International (text/call 1-800-944-4PPD) for 24-hr peer support and local provider referrals
7. Maintain basics: eat protein every 3-4 hrs, hydrate, and aim for one 4-hr block of uninterrupted sleep within each 24-hr cycle-ask someone else to handle one feeding if possible
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – EPDS-Style Narrative (not a formal Dx)

Identified symptoms/concerns:
- Anhedonia & reduced pleasure (Q1, Q2)
- Persistent low mood, “heavy/blah” most days (Q8)
- Excessive self-blame/guilt (Q3)
- Marked, often unprovoked anxiety and panic symptoms (Q4, Q5)
- Feeling overwhelmed and unable to cope with daily tasks (Q6)
- Sleep disturbance driven by intrusive worry (Q7)

Pattern:
Consistent dysphoric mood plus prominent anxiety symptoms; no suicidal ideation reported (Q10).

Risk indicators:
- Loss of enjoyment, mood-congruent sleep difficulties, excessive guilt
- Recurrent panic-type episodes, baseline worry about infant safety
- Functional impact (household tasks, social withdrawal)
- No self-harm thoughts at present

Screening observation:
Findings suggest clinically significant depressive and anxiety symptoms in the postpartum period; safety risk low today. Formal diagnostic assessment and discussion of support options recommended.
